capstone: CAPSTONE — The week-long engagement: act as the security manager of a fictional 120-person SaaS company preparing for its first enterprise customer security review. Deliverables: (1) a one-page risk summary naming the top 5 risks across at least 4 domains with a recommended disposition for each (accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid) and the business rationale; (2) a draft incident-response escalation page covering containment-vs-uptime tradeoffs; (3) an access-review calendar for the year with owners named for each review type; (4) a go/no-go recommendation on the next product release with the security evidence cited. Present your recommendations as if defending them to a skeptical CFO: every technical finding must end in a business consequence.
disclaimer: Original study guide keyed to public curriculum; course content itself lives at the source.

checkpoints: Your board will fund exactly one initiative this quarter: a $60k endpoint-protection upgrade OR a $60k vendor-risk-management program. The company has suffered one phishing compromise (contained) and is about to sign three new SaaS vendors. Write a half-page recommendation naming the initiative you fund, the risk you are accepting by defunding the other, and how you would measure success in 90 days.

A department head asks you to approve an exception allowing unencrypted USB drives for a field team that works where there is no network connectivity. Draft the exception request as the department head would submit it (business justification, compensating controls, expiry date) and then your decision memo as the security manager (approve, approve-with-conditions, or deny — with the residual risk stated plainly).

A regulator and a major customer each demand evidence of your risk process within 30 days, but your risk register is three years out of date. Write the two-week recovery plan: who you interview, what artifacts you produce, and what you will honestly tell each requester about gaps.
keyConcepts: Governance: policies, standards, procedures, and guidelines — and who signs each
Risk management lifecycle: identify, assess, treat (accept/mitigate/transfer/avoid), monitor
Qualitative vs quantitative risk analysis: when a simple matrix beats a dollar model
Business Impact Analysis (BIA): RTO, RPO, and critical-process ranking
Security roles: data owner, custodian, user, and the accountability chain
Personnel security: background checks, separation of duties, mandatory vacations, least privilege
Awareness and training: measuring behavior change, not completion rates
Ethics and professional conduct expectations for credentialed practitioners
labs: Draft a one-page acceptable-use policy for a fictional 50-person company: state scope, prohibited actions, monitoring notice, and consequences. Then write a separate one-paragraph exception process. Trade policies with a peer (or review your own after 48 hours) and mark every sentence you could not defend to an employee.

Build a risk register in a spreadsheet: 12 risks across people, process, and technology, each with likelihood, impact, a named owner, and a treatment decision. Include at least one accepted risk, one transferred risk, and one avoided risk. Write the residual-risk statement for the accepted risk as you would brief it to leadership.

Run a tabletop BIA: pick five business processes of a fictional online retailer, rank them by criticality, and assign RTO/RPO values with a one-sentence justification each. Then cut your recovery budget in half and re-rank — document what changed and why.

Write a supplier-security one-pager: the five questions you would ask any new SaaS vendor before procurement, the contract clauses you would require (right-to-audit, breach notification, data return), and how you would verify the answers without an on-site visit.
objectives: Write enforceable security policies, standards, and procedures and explain who approves each tier
Build and maintain a risk register: assess likelihood and impact, assign treatment, and brief residual risk to leadership
Conduct a business impact analysis and derive defensible RTO/RPO priorities
Design personnel-security controls (separation of duties, least privilege, termination procedures) and argue for them in business terms
modules.title: Module 1 — Security and Risk Management

checkpoints: Marketing wants to keep customer records indefinitely 'for analytics'; legal wants a 2-year retention ceiling. Draft the decision memo: state the classification of the data, who decides (owner vs custodian), the retention rule you recommend, and the control that makes each party's concern moot.

You inherit a shared drive where a predecessor stored customer PII alongside public marketing assets with identical permissions. Write the 30-day remediation plan: how you classify, who you consult before restricting access, and how you handle the discovery that two departed employees still have access.

A regulator asks how you would prove a specific record was destroyed. Describe the destruction workflow and the evidence artifact you would produce — then explain what changes if the record lives in a cloud provider's backups.
keyConcepts: Data classification levels and handling rules per level
Ownership vs custodianship: who decides, who implements
Data states: at rest, in transit, in use — and which controls fit each
Retention and legal hold: schedules, destruction, and defensibility
Privacy principles: purpose limitation, minimization, consent
Scoping and tailoring: applying controls proportionally to classification
Secure disposal: media sanitization methods and verification
Data remanence and why deletion is not destruction
labs: Write a four-tier data-classification scheme (with labels, examples, handling rules, and marking requirements) for a fictional healthcare-adjacent startup. Include a one-page quick-reference an employee could tape to a monitor.

Inventory your own home lab: list every place sensitive data lives (VMs, backups, cloud notes, password manager, phone), classify each item, and identify one item whose protection exceeds its classification and one that falls short. Fix the shortfall.

Run a disposal drill: document the sanitization method you would apply to three media types (spinning disk, SSD, paper), the verification step for each, and the record you would keep. Then actually sanitize a throwaway USB stick and photograph the evidence steps.

Draft a data-subject request procedure: the intake form, the identity-verification step, the search checklist across your systems, and the response template — with timelines you could actually meet solo.
objectives: Design a data-classification scheme and map handling controls to each level
Distinguish owner, custodian, and user responsibilities in a conflict scenario
Build defensible retention, legal-hold, and destruction procedures
Apply privacy principles (minimization, purpose limitation) to a real system design
modules.title: Module 2 — Asset Security

checkpoints: You must choose the cloud deployment model for a regulated workload: public cloud with strong controls vs private cloud on aging hardware the team knows well. Write the decision memo weighing shared-responsibility boundaries, key-management options, and exit strategy — then state your recommendation and the one assumption that would flip it.

A vendor proposes a 'military-grade' proprietary cipher for a new product. Write your reply: the evaluation questions you ask, the standard you require instead, and the business-risk sentence you would put in front of the product owner.

Your company is moving to zero-trust network access. Draft the phased rollout plan that keeps the help desk from drowning: which users migrate first, what breaks on day one, and how you measure that the new model is actually stricter than the VPN it replaces.
keyConcepts: Security models: Bell-LaPadula, Biba, Clark-Wilson — what each protects (confidentiality vs integrity)
Reference monitor, security kernel, and the trusted computing base idea
Cryptography selection: symmetric vs asymmetric, hashing, digital signatures, PKI trust
Key management lifecycle: generation, distribution, storage, rotation, destruction
Cloud service and deployment models and where responsibility shifts in each
Virtualization and container security boundaries
Physical and environmental controls as part of the architecture
Evaluation criteria for security products: what 'certified' actually claims
labs: Draw a segmented network architecture for a fictional company (office LAN, server segment, DMZ, guest Wi-Fi, management network): label every trust boundary, every firewall placement, and the traffic allowed across each boundary. Write the two-sentence justification for each boundary.

In your home lab, compare two TLS configurations on a test web server (e.g., weak legacy settings vs modern hardened settings) using a TLS scanner. Document which settings changed, what breaks with the hardened profile, and your recommendation for a public-facing vs internal-only service.

Design a key-management plan for a small team: where private keys live, how they are backed up, rotation schedule, and the revocation procedure when someone leaves. Implement it for one lab service and rotate the key once, documenting each step.

Evaluate one open-source security tool for adoption: write a one-page assessment covering trust (who maintains it), supportability, update cadence, and how you would detect if it were compromised. Conclude with adopt/reject and why.
objectives: Apply security models and design principles (least privilege, defense in depth, fail-secure) to a system architecture
Select appropriate cryptographic controls and manage keys through their lifecycle
Map shared-responsibility boundaries across cloud models and assign accountability
Evaluate security products and architectures against business requirements
modules.title: Module 3 — Security Architecture and Engineering

checkpoints: At 2 AM the monitoring system alerts on unusual outbound traffic from a database server to an external host. Write the first-hour decision log: what you check before waking anyone, the containment call you make at minute 30, and the evidence you preserve before the containment changes it.

The business wants to allow a new video-conferencing tool that uses peer-to-peer connections through the firewall. Write the network-security review: the ports/protocols question you ask the vendor, the firewall change you propose (and refuse), and the monitoring you add as a condition of approval.

Two branch offices need always-on connectivity. Compare site-to-site VPN vs private line in a half-page recommendation: the security properties that differ, the failure modes, and which you choose for a site handling payment data.
keyConcepts: OSI and TCP/IP models: where common attacks and controls operate
Firewalls: packet filter, stateful, application-layer, next-gen — and rule hygiene
VPNs: site-to-site vs remote access, tunneling, and endpoint trust
Wireless security: enterprise authentication vs pre-shared keys, rogue AP detection
Network segmentation and micro-segmentation rationale
Common attack patterns: spoofing, MitM, DoS/DDoS, DNS abuse
Secure communications: TLS, and what certificate validation actually proves
Network monitoring: what full-packet capture buys you that flow logs do not
labs: Build a host firewall ruleset (iptables/nftables or Windows Defender Firewall) for a lab server: default-deny, explicit allows, logging of drops. Test each rule with port scans from another VM, and document one rule you got wrong on the first pass and how the test exposed it.

Capture 10 minutes of your own lab traffic in Wireshark. Identify and annotate: a DNS exchange, a TLS handshake (and what is/isn't visible), one broadcast/multicast conversation, and any plaintext credential or token you can find on your own test services. Write the finding as a mini incident note.

Configure a site-to-site or client VPN between two lab VMs (e.g., WireGuard). Verify with captures on both the encrypted and unencrypted sides that payload is actually protected, then document the key-distribution step you would change for production.

Design a guest-Wi-Fi architecture for a small office: SSID strategy, authentication method, client isolation, bandwidth policy, and the firewall rules between guest and corporate. Implement the firewall portion in your lab router/VM and test isolation with two clients.
objectives: Design and validate firewall rulesets with default-deny posture and tested rule hygiene
Analyze packet captures to identify protocols, anomalies, and cleartext exposure
Deploy and verify encrypted tunnels (VPN/TLS) and explain what each protects against
Architect segmented networks including secure wireless for untrusted clients
modules.title: Module 4 — Communication and Network Security

checkpoints: A manager asks for standing administrator access 'to be efficient' for their 40-person team. Write your response: the alternative you offer (just-in-time elevation), the approval workflow, and the audit trail that makes the manager's request unnecessary — without using the word 'no' in the first paragraph.

HR reports a same-day termination of a privileged IT administrator who may be disgruntled. Write the 60-minute deprovisioning runbook in order: accounts, tokens, VPN, physical access, shared credentials — and the one step teams always forget.

The SSO provider has a 4-hour outage during month-end close. Write the after-action decision: do you keep the emergency bypass accounts you created, change their policy, or delete them — and what control prevents the bypass from becoming permanent?
keyConcepts: Identification, authentication, authorization, accountability — the full chain
MFA: factors, phishing-resistant options, and enrollment/recovery pitfalls
Access-control models: discretionary, mandatory, role-based, attribute-based
Provisioning lifecycle: joiner, mover, leaver — and orphaned accounts
Privileged access management: vaulting, session recording, just-in-time elevation
Single sign-on and federation: trust relationships and what breaks when they do
Access reviews and recertification: who attests, how often, what evidence
Accountability: why non-repudiation depends on the whole chain holding
labs: Perform a quarterly access review on your own lab: export every account on two systems, flag dormant accounts (>90 days), excessive privilege, and shared credentials. Write the review memo with revoke/retain decisions and a re-review date. Actually remove one dormant account.

Build an RBAC matrix for a fictional company: 6 roles × 8 systems, marking which access is standing vs just-in-time. Include the approval chain for granting the most privileged role, then role-play a request through it and find the step where it could be abused.

Harden authentication on your lab: enable MFA on every service that supports it, disable password-only logins where possible, and document the recovery procedure for a lost second factor. Then simulate the loss (lock yourself to the recovery path) and time how long recovery takes.

Audit service accounts in your home lab: list each one, its actual permission set vs what it needs, and reduce at least one over-privileged service account to least privilege. Document what broke and how you fixed the permission gap without restoring full rights.
objectives: Design a joiner/mover/leaver provisioning process with measurable SLAs
Implement least-privilege and privileged-access controls, including just-in-time elevation
Run a defensible periodic access review with documented revoke/retain decisions
Evaluate authentication architectures (MFA, SSO, federation) including failure and recovery modes
modules.title: Module 5 — Identity and Access Management (IAM)

checkpoints: Your vulnerability scan returns 400 findings across 60 servers with a two-person team and a 30-day patch window. Write the prioritization memo: your triage criteria (exploitability, asset criticality, exposure), the top-10 list with owners, and what you tell the auditor about the remaining 390.

A penetration-test proposal offers a no-holds-barred test of the production environment next week. Write your reply: the scope boundaries you require, the rules of engagement, the authorization paperwork, and the one test type you refuse on production — with the alternative you propose.

An internal audit finds the backup restores have never been tested. The backup admin says 'the jobs are green.' Write the finding as an auditor would (criteria, condition, cause, effect, recommendation) and then the manager's 90-day corrective-action plan.
keyConcepts: Vulnerability assessment vs penetration test vs security audit: different questions, different rules
Test strategies: black/white/gray box, and what each reveals
Vulnerability management lifecycle: discover, prioritize, remediate, verify
Security control testing: technical, administrative, and physical evidence
Log review and monitoring as an assessment input
Code review and testing perspectives for the security manager
Third-party and supply-chain assessment approaches
Metrics that matter: remediation SLAs, coverage, and repeat-findings rate
labs: Run an authenticated vulnerability scan (OpenVAS or Nessus Essentials) against two lab VMs you built with known-weak configurations. Triage the report: mark false positives with evidence, rank the true findings by exploitability × asset value, and write remediation tickets for the top 5 with verification steps.

Perform a controlled password-audit exercise on your own lab: extract hashes from a test VM you own, run a cracking tool with a small wordlist, and document which accounts fell and why. Then enforce the policy change that would have prevented the worst case and re-test.

Write a penetration-test scope document for a fictional engagement: targets, excluded systems, allowed techniques, communication plan, and emergency stop conditions. Include the written authorization template — and annotate three clauses that protect both the tester and the company.

Build a monthly security-metrics one-pager from your lab data: patch latency, scan coverage, open findings by age, and one trend line. Write the three-bullet executive summary you would attach, translating each metric into a business risk statement.
objectives: Scope and authorize security assessments (vuln scans, pen tests, audits) with proper rules of engagement
Triage vulnerability reports: validate findings, prioritize by risk, and drive remediation to closure
Write audit-grade findings and corrective-action plans
Build security metrics that translate technical results into management decisions
modules.title: Module 6 — Security Assessment and Testing

checkpoints: Ransomware is encrypting file shares at 3 AM; the on-call engineer wants to pull the network cable on the whole site, which would also kill the order-processing system during peak season. Write the incident-commander decision: contain now or contain surgically, who you wake, and the first three evidence-preservation orders.

A developer's laptop with customer data is stolen from a car. Write the first-24-hours plan: the notifications you owe (and to whom, in what order), the technical containment steps, and the question you ask legal before you say anything publicly.

Your SIEM fires 2,000 alerts a day and the analysts ignore most of them. Write the tuning proposal: which three alert classes you suppress or re-threshold first, the detection gap each change creates, and the compensating control you add for the riskiest gap.
keyConcepts: Incident response lifecycle: preparation through lessons learned
Digital forensics fundamentals: order of volatility, chain of custody
Logging: what to collect, retention, time synchronization, tamper protection
Business continuity vs disaster recovery: plans, roles, and testing methods
SOC operations: triage, escalation, and alert tuning
Patch and vulnerability operations: change control under pressure
Physical and personnel security operations
Resilience: redundancy, backups, and tested recovery
labs: Stand up centralized logging in your lab (e.g., Wazuh, Graylog, or rsyslog + a parser): forward logs from at least three sources, write one detection rule for brute-force logins, and tune it until a simulated attack fires exactly one alert. Document the false positives you eliminated.

Write a one-page incident-response playbook for 'suspected compromised workstation': roles, first-30-minutes checklist, evidence-preservation steps, and escalation criteria. Then tabletop it solo against a scenario where the workstation belongs to the CFO during earnings week — note what the playbook missed.

Perform a backup-and-restore drill: back up a lab VM, deliberately break it, and restore from backup while timing each phase. Document the RTO you actually achieved vs the one you assumed, and write the gap as a finding with a corrective action.

Run a forensic-preservation exercise on a test VM you own: capture memory and disk images in forensically sound order, hash everything, and write the chain-of-custody log. Then explain in writing what you would do differently on a live production system you cannot take offline.
objectives: Operate the incident-response lifecycle: detect, contain, eradicate, recover, and learn
Build and tune detection content (logging, alerting) against false-positive pressure
Execute and measure backup, continuity, and disaster-recovery procedures
Apply forensic fundamentals: volatility order, imaging, hashing, chain of custody
modules.title: Module 7 — Security Operations

checkpoints: A critical vulnerability is announced in a library your flagship product ships, on the eve of a major release. Write the ship/no-ship memo: the exploitability questions you ask engineering, the mitigations that would let you ship, and the residual-risk statement the CTO signs.

A security researcher emails you a vulnerability report with a 90-day disclosure deadline and a proof of concept. Draft the response plan: intake, validation, severity assignment, remediation timeline, and the coordinated-disclosure reply — including what you do if engineering disputes the severity.

Your team wants to adopt an AI coding assistant. Write the secure-use policy: what code it may touch, what data it may see, the review gate before AI-generated code merges, and the one prohibition you hold even if it slows the team down.
keyConcepts: Secure SDLC phases: where security activities inject into each phase
Threat modeling: assets, attackers, and abuse cases before code exists
Common software vulnerabilities and their root causes (input handling, auth flaws, crypto misuse)
Secure coding practices: validation, output encoding, safe error handling
Security testing in the pipeline: SAST, DAST, SCA, and what each misses
Change and release management from the security perspective
Database and application-layer controls
DevSecOps: shifting security left without stopping delivery
labs: Threat-model a small application you build or already run: draw the data-flow diagram, list trust boundaries, and enumerate threats per boundary using STRIDE or a simple attacker-goal list. Pick the top 3 threats and write the concrete mitigation for each — then implement one.

Do a guided code review of an intentionally vulnerable practice app (e.g., a deliberately insecure demo app run locally): find and document 5 vulnerabilities with severity, exploit scenario, and fix. Write each finding the way you would in a professional report — no snark, just facts and remediation.

Add security gates to a toy CI pipeline: a linter/security scanner (SAST), dependency scanning (SCA), and a secrets-detection step. Commit a deliberately vulnerable change and a leaked test secret; verify each gate catches its target, then document the false positive you had to suppress and why the suppression is safe.

Write a secure-coding standard excerpt for your team: input-validation rules, authentication requirements, cryptography rules (approved algorithms, no homegrown crypto), and logging requirements. Keep it to two pages an engineer would actually read — then test it by reviewing a 100-line script against it.
objectives: Integrate security activities into each SDLC phase (requirements through decommissioning)
Threat-model an application and derive concrete, implementable mitigations
Evaluate software vulnerabilities and recommend fixes in business-priority order
Design DevSecOps pipeline gates (SAST/DAST/SCA/secrets) that catch real issues without blocking delivery
modules.title: Module 8 — Software Development Security

objectives: Build practitioner-level judgment across all 8 CISSP CBK domains through scenario-driven study, not memorization
Practice the managerial decision-making the exam rewards: risk tradeoffs, prioritization under constraints, and business-aligned recommendations
Develop hands-on fluency with the tools and artifacts of each domain in a home lab (policies, registers, firewall rules, packet analysis, scans, logs, pipeline gates)
Learn to brief technical findings to non-technical leadership: every conclusion ends in a business consequence

Note: CISSP is a credential for experienced security practitioners. ISC2 requires verified professional experience for certification — check the current requirements on the official ISC2 page before planning your path.
